# Data Analytics

## Predictive Analytics

### Forecasting Problem and Baselines

The task is to predict **taxi demand per hexagon and 4-hour window**, using only information available before the window begins: time of day, day of week, weather forecast, and location.
A dispatcher scheduling tomorrow's shifts doesn't have tomorrow's actual counts, so the models use no lagged demand.
Trip counts are heavily skewed (a few downtown cells see hundreds of pickups per window, most outer cells single digits), so we train on log-transformed counts and report all metrics back on the trip scale.
The grid is randomly split 50 / 20 / 30 into training, validation, and test data.
The test set is touched once, for the final numbers.

Two naive benchmarks give the results business meaning.
The *per-cell mean*, the historical average per hexagon and window, scores MAE 67.18 trips.
*Climatology*, the average per hexagon, hour, and weekday-vs-weekend, scores MAE 25.63.
Climatology is the hurdle that matters.
It's what an operator gets from a simple lookup schedule, so a model earns its complexity only by beating it.

### Support Vector Machine

We tuned a Support Vector Machine for regression across kernel types and regularisation settings on a validation subsample; the search and its intermediate results are in @sec-app-models.
The best configuration, an RBF kernel with C = 10, confirms that the link between weather, calendar, and demand is non-linear.
@tbl-svm-results shows the final test-set results on 41,367 grid cells.

| Model | MAE | RMSE | R$^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-cell mean | 67.18 | 216.97 | 0.633 |
| Climatology | 25.63 | 93.19 | 0.932 |
| SVR (RBF) | **24.33** | **88.05** | **0.940** |

: SVR test-set performance compared to baselines. {#tbl-svm-results}

The SVR beats both baselines, but its margin over climatology is thin: MAE 24.33 against 25.63, roughly 5 %.
Without access to recent actual counts, most of what it can learn is the seasonal pattern climatology already encodes.
The 5 % it adds comes from weather and calendar interactions a fixed schedule can't represent.
The error is also unevenly distributed.
The model is accurate in the many low-demand cells but under-predicts the busy downtown and airport hexagons where forecasts matter most, a known artefact of training on compressed log counts (decomposition in @sec-app-models).

We also tested the tuned model across coarser and finer grids, since the granularity choice itself is a business decision.
Finer cells cut the absolute error per cell (from 73 to 31 trips MAE at 4-hour windows) simply because each cell holds fewer trips, while explained variance stays around 0.9; the full sweep is in @sec-app-models.
Resolution 6 with 4-hour windows remains the working choice.
Census tracts (roughly 800 units instead of 27) would multiply sparsity without operational benefit.

### Feedforward Neural Network

We trained a feedforward neural network on the same grid and features, so the two models are directly comparable.
A grid search over architectures, learning rates, and optimisers (detailed in @sec-app-models) selected a network with two hidden layers of 256 neurons, trained with the Adam optimiser.
@tbl-nn-results shows the final test-set results.

| Model | MAE | RMSE | R$^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Climatology | 24.42 | 87.22 | 0.937 |
| Neural network | **21.16** | **80.78** | **0.946** |

: Neural network test-set performance compared to the climatology baseline. {#tbl-nn-results}

The network also beats climatology, and by a wider margin: MAE 21.16 against 24.42, a 13 % improvement.
It captures more of the demand structure beyond the weekly rhythm, in particular how weather, time, and location interact.
A residual bias of $-8.25$ trips shows the extreme downtown peaks are still partly missed.
Those spikes come from events the data can't see, such as concerts and sports fixtures, and would need an event calendar to forecast reliably.

The model's operational output is an on-demand forecast for any combination of location, time, weather, and day type.
Queried for an outer-city hexagon on a rainy Sunday in July, it predicts demand rising from 34.4 trips at 10:00 to a peak of 37.3 at midday, then easing to 20.4 by 18:00.
That's about 282 trips across the window, following the leisure-weekend build-up seen in the descriptive analysis.

### Model Comparison

Both models run on the same resolution 6 grid with 4-hour windows, each measured against its own climatology baseline (the notebooks use different random splits, hence the slightly different baseline values):

| Model | Setting | Climatology MAE | Model MAE | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SVR (RBF) | H3 res. 6, 4 h windows | 25.63 | 24.33 | **Better** (+5 %) |
| Neural network | H3 res. 6, 4 h windows | 24.42 | 21.16 | **Better** (+13 %) |

: Each model's performance relative to the climatology baseline. {#tbl-model-comparison}

The neural network wins for two structural reasons.
It trains on the full dataset while the SVR, which scales poorly, had to learn from a small subsample.
And it learns feature interactions jointly, where the SVR applies one fixed transformation to every input.
Both beat the seasonal schedule, but the network improves on it by roughly two and a half times as much.
For an operator positioning vehicles under changing weather or on atypical weekdays, that responsiveness is the point: a seasonal average says nothing about whether tomorrow's rainy Monday will run busier than a dry one.
